paragraphs.heading: The sunlight zone
paragraphs.text: The epipelagic zone, also called the photic, euphotic or sunlight zone, is the top layer of a body of water, the part that sunlight reaches. That light lets phytoplankton, tiny plants that float in the water with little or no way to move themselves, carry out photosynthesis. Below it lies the aphotic zone, a region of permanent darkness that holds most of the ocean's water.

paragraphs.heading: Where most sea life lives
paragraphs.text: Although it is the smallest ocean zone by volume, this layer is home to most life in the sea. About 90% of marine life lives here, in water roughly 200 meters deep, and 95% of the ocean's photosynthesis happens here too. Plenty of solar energy means photosynthesis outpaces respiration in this layer, and phytoplankton grow very fast. Go deeper, past the light, and there is little or no phytoplankton left.

paragraphs.heading: Who lives here
paragraphs.text: The phytoplankton include diatoms, dinoflagellates, cyanobacteria and coccolithophores. The consumers here are zooplankton, some eating plants and some eating meat. Copepods, small crustaceans, are found all through the layer. The biggest and most visible animals are the nekton, creatures such as fish, squid and crabs that swim under their own power, though they are the fewest in number. Because phytoplankton are the first link in the food chain, whatever happens to them ripples out to other species.

paragraphs.heading: How deep the light goes
paragraphs.text: By definition, the zone ends where light has dropped to 1% of its strength at the surface. So its depth depends on how clear the water is. It can be just a few centimetres in very murky lakes and around 200 meters in the open ocean. It also shifts with the seasons, and it often gets shallower when phytoplankton are booming and clouding the water.

paragraphs.heading: Short on nutrients
paragraphs.text: Living things take up so much here that nutrient levels in this layer are fairly low. When the water column is very stable, phytoplankton can run short of nutrients. Upwelling carries nutrients up from deep water and boosts phytoplankton growth, and Ekman transport adds more. Dead organisms start to decay in this zone, and once they sink into the darkness below, they become the most important food source for deep-sea life.

paragraphs.heading: A built-in clock
paragraphs.text: Animals in the sunlight zone use the daily swing between light and dark as a key signal. Fish such as herrings and sardines time their migrations by dusk and dawn, so the layer gives its residents a sense of time.
